content.title: About
content.content: Toasted rye bread is a whole‑grain loaf made from rye flour and lightly toasted until the crust turns golden. It has a distinctive mildly sour taste, dense crumb, and a fragrant, crunchy crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rye bread is traditionally considered healthier than wheat bread because it contains more fiber.
Toasting enhances aroma and creates a crisp crust while slowing down spoilage.
In many Eastern European countries rye toast is used as a base for open‑face sandwiches with herring, smoked fish, or pâté.
Rye flour has a lower glycemic index, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.
Traditional rye loaves are often baked in steam ovens, giving them a moist interior.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain gut health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Rye bread provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps control blood glucose levels, beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides magnesium, iron, and phosphorus important for bones and nerve function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Rye flour contains phenolic compounds that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Rye bread contains gluten and is not suitable for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Some commercial versions may be high in salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Toasted rye can be slightly more acidic, which may cause discomfort for those with gastritis.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted rye bread works well for open‑face sandwiches, avocado toast, soup croutons, and snack bites. Spread with butter, cream cheese, or hummus. Serve the toast while the crust is still crisp for best texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, wrap tightly in foil and refrigerate for up to a week or freeze in an airtight bag for up to 3 months. Re‑toast before serving to restore crispness.

chicken-leg-drumstick-and-thigh-fried-co.title: Chicken leg, drumstick and thigh, fried, coated, skin/coating eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken legs, drumsticks and thighs are the dark meat portions of a chicken, rich in meat and fat. When deep‑fried they develop a crispy coating, and the skin becomes flavorful and edible. This dish is common in fast‑food restaurants and home cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark chicken meat contains more iron and zinc than white meat.
Frying at 175‑190 °C creates a golden crust while keeping the interior juicy.
Chicken legs are a staple in Asian cuisines, often glazed with teriyaki or sweet‑spicy sauces.
Coating can be made from breadcrumbs, flour, spices, and sometimes corn starch for extra crunch.
When properly prepared, the skin turns fully edible and adds a distinctive aroma.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Dark chicken meat provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are essential for immune function and oxygen transport.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for nervous system health and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: The fat in dark meat includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can support heart health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and a crunchy coating helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant calories; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Potential trans fats
items.content: Using old or overheated oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Coatings often contain salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you have hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot as a standalone snack, in burgers, with dipping sauces (barbecue, mayo, garlic), or tossed in salads. Sprinkle with fresh herbs, lemon juice, or your favorite spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pieces in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C; reheat in the oven to restore crispness after thawing.

pizza-with-meat-and-fruit-medium-crust.title: Pizza with meat and fruit, medium crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with meat and fruit is an original combination of juicy meat (usually ham, sausage or chicken) and sweet fruits (pineapple, apple, pear). A medium‑thick crust provides a balance between a crispy edge and a soft interior. The pizza is suitable for family dinners as well as festive gatherings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The meat‑and‑fruit pairing is popular in Hawaiian cuisine, where the classic “Hawaiian” pizza features ham and pineapple.
Fruits add natural sweetness and help soften the salty flavor of the meat.
Medium crust is typically baked at 220‑240 °C for 10‑12 minutes, yielding a golden crust while keeping the topping moist.
Pizza with fruit is often served with a light tomato base, sometimes enhanced with barbecue sauce for extra depth.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from fruit
items.content: Fruits contribute vitamin C, potassium and dietary fiber, supporting immunity and digestion.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: Carbohydrates from the crust, protein from the meat, and simple sugars from the fruit deliver both quick and sustained energy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Meat‑and‑fruit pizza can be calorie‑dense due to cheese, crust and fatty meats; moderation is advised.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to dairy, gluten in the crust, or specific types of meat.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Processed meats and sauces often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should choose lower‑sodium options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into individual slices. Fresh basil or arugula can be added after baking for aroma. Optionally drizzle with a light yogurt sauce or spicy chili.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill pan to restore a crispy crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Rob Roy is a classic cocktail made with Scotch whisky, sweet vermouth, and Angostura bitters. It was created in the early 1900s in New York, inspired by the popular operetta “Rob Roy.” The drink is known for its smooth, slightly sweet and spicy flavor with a hint of bitterness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Rob Roy recipe appeared in the 1900s at the Waldorf Astoria bar in New York.
The cocktail is named after the Scottish poet Robert “Rob” Roy MacGregor, known as Rob Roy.
There are several variations: Sweet Rob Roy (with red vermouth), Dry Rob Roy (with dry vermouth) and Perfect Rob Roy (half sweet, half dry vermouth).
Angostura bitters, used in the recipe, were created in the 1850s in Barbados and remain one of the most popular cocktail bitters.
Rob Roy is traditionally served in a cocktail glass, though a martinez glass is sometimes used for a more refined presentation.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: A small amount of whisky can have a calming effect due to the alcohol’s mild sedative properties.

items.title: Contains antioxidants from vermouth
items.content: Both sweet and dry vermouth are wine‑based and contain polyphenols that act as antioxidants.

items.title: Angostura bitters provide aromatic herbs
items.content: Bitters often include extracts of bitter herbs traditionally used in herbal medicine.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: The cocktail contains ethanol, so it should be consumed responsibly and avoided during pregnancy, driving, or liver disease.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet vermouth adds sugar, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or low‑carb diets.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to the herbal components in Angostura bitters.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Combine 45 ml Scotch whisky, 20 ml sweet or dry vermouth, and a few dashes of Angostura bitters in a mixing glass with ice. Stir, strain into a chilled cocktail glass, and garnish with a cherry or an orange twist. Serve neat, without ice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Alcoholic ingredients (whisky, vermouth, bitters) should be kept in tightly sealed bottles in a cool, dark place. Once opened, vermouth is best stored in the refrigerator, while bitters can remain at room temperature away from direct light.
